children: Shares of Seagate Technology tanked Tuesday as the hard-drive maker's strong quarterly earnings weren't enough for investors.

Wall Street has scrutinized Seagate more heavily in recent months after the stock's blistering run to start the year. The record-breaking profitability Seagate delivered in the fiscal first quarter was therefore a baseline — not a signal to buy.
Seagate stock tumbled 7.3% to $619.36 after hours Tuesday, having jumped 3.7% in regular trading. Shares are now down 43% from their all-time closing high on June 22.

Seagate reported adjusted earnings of $7.68 a share for the quarter ended Oct. 2, up from $2.61 a year ago and surpassing Wall Street's call for $7.45, per FactSet. Revenue rose 61% year over year to $4.23 billion, above analysts' consensus forecast of $4.15 billion.

Guidance also beat Wall Street's expectations. The company expects adjusted earnings of $9.20 a share, plus or minus 20 cents, on revenue of $4.8 billion in the second quarter. Analysts had anticipated earnings per share of $8.66 and revenue of $4.5 billion.
This is breaking news. Read a preview of Seagate's earnings below and check back for more analysis soon.

Shares of Seagate Technology have reversed course after a hot start to the year, and the hard-drive maker likely needs a pristine fiscal first-quarter earnings report on Tuesday afternoon to get back on track.

Seagate's earnings report comes less than a week after its primary rival, Western Digital, beat earnings expectations to no avail. Western Digital stock sank amid questions about rising capital expenditures and the potential for new hard drive supply. Seagate stock followed.
Shares of Seagate are still up nearly 200% to $657.17 from a year ago. However, they have fallen 40% from a record closing high on June 22, 2026.

Seagate has ridden the artificial intelligence wave to record profit. AI requires and produces massive amounts of data, which companies can store on hard-disk drives, or HDDs. Seagate and Western Digital are the only U.S. HDD sellers, and they taking advantage of tight supply by signing long-term contracts at high margins with customers.

The only issue is that the data storage business is traditionally cyclical, and Wall Street will get spooked by any indicator that demand may falter or supply may expand. Case in point: Seagate stock tanked earlier this month following a report that Japanese competitor Toshiba was planning to boost production capacity.

A simple beat-and-raise may not be enough for Seagate, as Western Digital just proved. Analysts polled by FactSet expect Seagate to report adjusted earnings of $7.45 a share for the quarter ended Oct. 2, up from $2.61 a year ago. Revenue is expected to rise 58% from a year ago, to $4.15 billion.
Pricing will also be top of mind for investors.

"We believe that the majority of STX's nearline HDD volume is under build-to-order contracts," Wamsi Mohan, an analyst at BofA Securities, wrote in a research note last week. "As these come up for renewal, we expect STX to increase pricing."

BofA sees prices and margins continuing to expand "well into 2028," giving Seagate stock the opportunity to recover from its recent malaise. The firm lifted its price target for Seagate shares to $1,200 from $1,150 and reiterated a Buy rating.
All told, 83% of analysts tracked by FactSet rate Seagate the equivalent of a Buy, and the average price target remains over $1,100.
